## Proof

**Yes**, $H \cap SL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ has finite index in $SL_n(\mathbb{Z})$.

The argument rests on a basic group-theoretic fact and does not depend on the specific nature of the extension $\hat{\mathbb{Z}}$.

### Setup

Since $\hat{\mathbb{Z}}$ is an extension of $\mathbb{Z}$, there is an injective ring homomorphism $\iota: \mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow \hat{\mathbb{Z}}$. (For the profinite completion, injectivity follows from the residual finiteness of $\mathbb{Z}$; for any algebraic extension ring, injectivity is part of the definition of "extension.")

Applying $\iota$ entry-wise to matrices yields a group homomorphism
$$\phi: SL_n(\mathbb{Z}) \longrightarrow SL_n(\hat{\mathbb{Z}}),$$
which is injective (since $\iota$ is injective, two distinct integer matrices remain distinct over $\hat{\mathbb{Z}}$). We identify $SL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ with its image $\phi(SL_n(\mathbb{Z})) \leq SL_n(\hat{\mathbb{Z}})$.

### Key group-theoretic lemma

**Lemma.** Let $G'$ be a group, $G \leq G'$ a subgroup, and $H \leq G'$ a subgroup of finite index. Then $G \cap H$ has finite index in $G$, and moreover
$$[G : G \cap H] \leq [G' : H].$$

*Proof of Lemma.* Consider the map on coset spaces
$$G / (G \cap H) \longrightarrow G' / H, \qquad g(G \cap H) \longmapsto gH.$$
This map is well-defined: if $g_1, g_2$ lie in the same $(G \cap H)$-coset, then $g_1^{-1}g_2 \in G \cap H \subseteq H$, so $g_1 H = g_2 H$. It is injective: if $g_1 H = g_2 H$ with $g_1, g_2 \in G$, then $g_1^{-1}g_2 \in H \cap G$, so $g_1$ and $g_2$ are in the same $(G \cap H)$-coset. Therefore $G/(G \cap H)$ injects into the finite set $G'/H$, giving $[G : G \cap H] \leq [G' : H] < \infty$. $\square$

### Application

Set $G' = SL_n(\hat{\mathbb{Z}})$, $G = SL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ (viewed as a subgroup via $\phi$), and $H$ the given finite-index subgroup. By hypothesis, $[G' : H] < \infty$. By the lemma,
$$[SL_n(\mathbb{Z}) : SL_n(\mathbb{Z}) \cap H] \leq [SL_n(\hat{\mathbb{Z}}) : H] < \infty.$$

### Conclusion

$H \cap SL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ has finite index in $SL_n(\mathbb{Z})$, with the index bounded above by $[SL_n(\hat{\mathbb{Z}}) : H]$. The result holds for any $n \geq 1$ (the case $n=1$ being trivial since $SL_1$ is the trivial group) and does not depend on any special property of the extension $\hat{\mathbb{Z}}$ beyond the injectivity of $\mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow \hat{\mathbb{Z}}$.
